nameStory: The 'cutleaf' in this anemone's name comes from its deeply divided, almost feathery leaves that look like they've been cut with tiny scissors. The word 'anemone' comes from the Greek word for 'windflower,' because these delicate blooms dance and sway in the slightest breeze.
description: Cutleaf anemone is a delicate wildflower that stands 6-16 inches tall on slender stems. Its most striking feature is its finely divided, lacy leaves that create an almost fern-like appearance. The solitary white, pink, or pale purple flowers have 5-8 petal-like sepals surrounding a fuzzy yellow center, blooming from late spring through summer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut into narrow, thread-like segments that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, creating an intricate lacy pattern that's unmistakable among New England wildflowers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single flowers with 5-8 white, pink, or pale purple petal-like sepals (actually sepals, not true petals) surrounding a prominent fuzzy yellow center of stamens

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing perennial forming small clumps, with flowers held on leafless stems that rise above the basal rosette of deeply divided leaves

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Forms a round, fluffy seed head with silky-haired seeds that catch the wind, similar to a small dandelion puff but more compact

habitat: This rare wildflower is found in dry, open areas including prairies, rocky slopes, and sandy soils in New England's most northern regions. It prefers well-drained sites with full sun to partial shade, often growing among grasses and other prairie wildflowers. Given its extreme rarity in New England with only 10 recorded observations, it's most likely encountered in specialized habitats like calcareous outcrops or remnant prairie openings.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as distinctive lacy leaf rosettes, with the intricate cut-leaf pattern already visible and helpful for identification even before blooming begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with delicate flowers appearing from June through August, followed by the formation of fluffy, round seed heads that persist for weeks.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads mature and disperse, while the basal leaves may persist and turn slightly bronze or purple before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground parts for identification until spring emergence.

funFact: This tiny wildflower has one of the most impressive geographic ranges of any North American plant, somehow thriving from the Arctic tundra of Alaska all the way down to the high deserts of New Mexico and even parts of South America—yet it's incredibly rare in New England!
confusionNotes: The finely divided leaves might remind you of wild carrot or yarrow, but cutleaf anemone's leaves are much more delicate and thread-like, and it has solitary flowers rather than umbrella-shaped clusters. Remember: if the leaves look like green lace and there's just one flower per stem, you've likely found this rare anemone.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'anemone,' this plant is unrelated to sea anemones—it's named for the Greek wind god Anemos because the flowers sway gracefully in breezes. Its extreme rarity in New England likely reflects that we're at the very edge of its natural range, where it struggles to compete with our region's lusher vegetation.
compareHints: Unlike its New England relatives tall thimbleweed and cylindrical thimbleweed, cutleaf anemone has much more finely divided, lacy leaves rather than broader, coarsely toothed ones. It's also much smaller overall and has solitary flowers, while the thimbleweeds are taller plants with different flower arrangements and less ornate foliage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tall thimbleweed stands out from its relatives by its height and that distinctive whorl of three deeply cut leaves halfway up the stem.
Cylindrical thimbleweed differs from its relative tall thimbleweed by its distinctly elongated, narrow seed head versus the latter's more rounded, globe-shaped one.
